papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Fully Distributed Gaussian Process Regression
papers.summary: Although distributed Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables multiple agents to jointly learn a model of the target function, its collaborative nature poses a risk of private data leakage. To address this, we propose a privacy-preserving fully distributed GPR protocol based on secure multi-party computation, which hides each agent's individual contribution from semi-honest coalitions of bounded size, beyond what is implied by the aggregated value. Building upon a secure distributed average consensus algorithm, it guarantees that each agent's local model practically converges to the same global model obtained by the standard distributed GPR. Formal privacy guarantees are established within the simulation based security paradigm. The protocol is further extended to privacy-preserving optimization of kernel hyperparameters, which is critical yet often overlooked in the literature. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed method.

papers.title: Operator-in-the-Loop Rolling Dispatch for Damage-Assessment Crews Under Partial Storm Information
papers.summary: Natural disasters often inflict severe damage on distribution grids. Rapid, reliable damage assessment (DA) is essential for storm restoration, yet most optimization work targets repair dispatch after faults are identified. This paper presents a production, rolling horizon DA crew allocation system deployed across multiple U.S. states in Eversource Energy's service territory and used during live storms. The method implements a sequential k-job assignment policy per available crew, executed on a fixed cadence and on operators' control. The objective jointly prioritizes critical facilities and customer impact while controlling travel time on the actual road network via the Google Maps API. A key constraint is the absence of live crew GPS; we infer crew locations from the last confirmed DA site and robustify travel estimates for staleness, yielding stable recommendations without continuous tracking. The operator remains in the loop with controls to limit churn and to publish a feasible plan. Using data from the March 7 New Hampshire storm with 90 moderate outages and seven DA crews, we observe shorter time to first assessment, fewer revisits with reduced distance traveled. To our knowledge, this is among the first multi-state enterprise integrated deployments to treat DA crews as a first-class optimized resource in storm restoration.

papers.title: Leaky Coaxial Cable based Generalized Pinching-Antenna Systems with Dual-Port Feeding
papers.summary: By leveraging the distributed leakage radiation of leaky coaxial cables (LCXs), the concept of pinching antennas can be generalized from the conventional high-frequency waveguide based architectures to cable based structures in lower-frequency scenarios. This paper investigates an LCX based generalized pinching-antenna system with dual-port feeding. By enabling bidirectional excitation along each cable, the proposed design significantly enhances spatial degrees of freedom. A comprehensive channel model is developed to characterize intra-cable attenuation, bidirectional phase progression, slot based radiation, and wireless propagation. Based on this model, both analog and hybrid beamforming frameworks are studied with the objective of maximizing the minimum achievable data rate. For analog transmission, slot activation, port selection, and power allocation are jointly optimized using matching theory, coalitional games, and bisection based power control. For hybrid transmission, zero-forcing (ZF) digital precoding is incorporated to eliminate inter-user interference, thereby simplifying slot activation and enabling closed-form optimal power allocation. Simulation results demonstrate that dual-port feeding provides notable performance gains over single-port LCX systems and fixed-antenna benchmarks, validating the effectiveness of the proposed beamforming and resource allocation designs under various transmit power levels and cable parameters.

papers.title: System Design Framework for Distributed Space Antennas Using Electromagnetic Formation Flight
papers.summary: Distributed space antennas using electromagnetic formation flight (EMFF) are a promising architecture for large-aperture, long-life space communication systems. Their system design, however, is governed by coupled constraints on antenna performance, satellite mass, power generation, coil geometry, and formation-keeping power. This paper proposes a system-level design framework for EMFF-based distributed space antennas. It links phased-array requirements with satellite and formation-system sizing for a static grid under a fixed total system mass. Before system-level optimization, distributed-control simulations are used to derive a control index that quantifies the formation-maintenance requirement. This index is integrated into an optimization problem with a user-defined objective and sizing, power, coil, and sidelobe-envelope constraints. Parametric case studies examine the margin magnetic moment, prescribed transmit power, and large inter-satellite spacing. Results show that increasing system mass improves footprint reduction or effective isotropic radiated power only while satellite-level design headroom remains. In direct-to-device cases with 0.15-m spacing, generated power and coil-geometry constraints dominate the feasible aperture. In the 0.30-m large-spacing case, the required coil burden can exceed satellite-level mass, size, and power capacities, making the design infeasible despite favorable communication performance. Higher-fidelity simulations of representative designs evaluate formation maintenance under nonlinear $J_2$ dynamics and antenna gain with mutual coupling, further supporting the framework's usefulness for preliminary design. The proposed framework enables the design and evaluation of feasible static grid-based EMFF distributed antennas under coupled antenna, satellite, and control constraints.

papers.title: Task-Based Evaluation of Raw Radar Data Compression: A Pre-Registered Study of Where Classical Codecs Fail to Preserve Target Detection, and Why
papers.summary: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) systems collect raw I/Q echo data at rates that exceed downlink capacity; fielded systems compress onboard with block-adaptive quantization (BAQ/FDBAQ). Proposed replacements, including learned compression, are evaluated with image-quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, SQNR); none measures whether the data still supports its operational use. We introduce a task-based evaluation methodology for raw radar compression, with a published pre-registration trail: codecs are scored after SAR focusing against a two-sided criterion -- a CFAR detection-retention floor and a spurious-detection budget at matched threshold -- using frozen task models trained once on uncompressed data. On Sentinel-1 stripmap Level-0 data the evaluation brackets the fielded FDBAQ operating point at the resolution of the BAQ grid (3-bit BAQ sustains utility at 6.12 bits per complex sample; 2-bit does not), with a reported lattice artifact found to change retention by at most 0.004. Under the final plane-mapping rule no classical configuration sustains utility below 4.86 bits per complex sample on this scene. Energy concentration after focusing delivers the predicted retention gain (0.888 vs 0.691 at 2 bits) but converts it into target-adjacent false alarms for wavelet and block-transform codecs alike: a retention-only rule certifies focused-domain JPEG2000 at 4 bits while it produces 2.5 times the tolerable spurious count. On AFRL Gotcha GMTI data (airborne, never compressed onboard) the frontier is bracketed at 7.4-8.0 bits per complex sample and the same trade reappears; on an Umbra spotlight image JPEG2000 passes the retention floor at 2, 1, and 0.5 bits while producing 10-14 times the spurious budget. We report the full pre-registration trail, including the chronology of the criterion's two clauses, one retracted overclaim, and a bounded negative result for a small learned codec.

papers.title: Short-Range Microwave Interprobe Coupling in a Brain-Mimicking Phantom and Ex-Vivo Brain
papers.summary: Objectives: Short-range wireless links (microwave range) between closely spaced devices in brain tissue are relevant to neural interfaces and intracranial sensing, yet the change in coupling between two such devices caused by a finite volume of brain-like tissue has rarely been measured directly. Technology or Method: This work characterizes a printed, microstrip-fed, parasitic-strip-loaded tapered-slot coupling probe in which only a partially inserted 12-mm wire enters the medium, while the printed structure remains outside. Results: Two fabricated probes showed a measured free-space -10-dB reflection band of 5.78 to 6.86 GHz and a fractional bandwidth of approximately 17.1%, consistent with full-wave simulation. In a controlled two-probe experiment, a homogeneous agar-gelatin-saline brain-mimicking phantom was introduced and removed while the probe arrangement and measurement conditions were retained. Introducing the phantom increased the measured transmission coefficient near 6.3 GHz by approximately 16 dB, and this differential was reproduced across repeated trials. More than five measurements in ex vivo goat brain followed the phantom transmission response within approximately 1.5 dB across the 5.78-6.86-GHz band. Time-domain analysis of the phantom-present link gave a system root-mean-square delay spread of approximately 210 ps. Full-wave dosimetry predicted a peak 1-g-averaged specific absorption rate of 1.05 W/kg for approximately 0.49 W accepted power. Conclusions and Clinical or Biological Impact: These results provide an experimentally validated reference for short-range probe coupling in brain-like media and support phantom-based bench evaluation of minimally invasive intracranial probes before in vivo studies.

papers.title: Controller-Agnostic Runtime Safety Certificates for Tool-Using AI Agents via Data-Driven Robust Reachability
papers.summary: Software agents built on large language models act by issuing tool calls, some of which cannot be undone. To control theory the model is an opaque feedback controller, replaced every few months, whose closed loop cannot be analyzed directly. We propose a runtime filter, or shield, between any such controller and its environment that certifies a bound on the probability of reaching an unsafe condition during a bounded task. Given a predicate abstraction and candidate successor sets, everything else comes from logs: the loop becomes a finite controlled Markov chain, the estimated kernel is surrounded by a distribution-free confidence region, and robust reach-avoid value iteration runs over it. The certificate is probably approximately correct and uniform over controllers respecting the filter, so one model may replace another without recomputation. In all tested datasets the true risk stayed within certificate and budget; in a file-system sandbox the filter stays sound against a hazard the logs barely covered, where a plug-in baseline certifies safety and fails; and it holds seven controllers, three of them open-weights models, to zero unsafe outcomes in 1050 episodes.

papers.title: Bistatic Target Detection by Exploiting Both Deterministic Pilots and Unknown Random Data Payloads
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) plays a crucial role in 6G, enabling innovative applications such as drone surveillance, urban air mobility, and low-altitude logistics. However, the hybrid ISAC signal, which comprises deterministic pilot and random data payload components, poses challenges for target detection due to two reasons: 1) these two components cause coupled shifts in both the mean and variance of the received signal, and 2) the random data payloads are typically unknown to the sensing receiver in the bistatic setting. Unfortunately, these challenges could not be tackled by existing target detection algorithms. In this paper, a generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT)-based detector is derived by leveraging the known deterministic pilots and the statistical characteristics of the unknown random data payloads. Due to the analytical intractability of exact performance characterization, we perform an asymptotic analysis for the false alarm probability and detection probability of the proposed detector. The results reveal a deterministic-random trade-off: the deterministic pilots enhance detection through a target-induced mean shift, while the random data payloads provide an additional covariance-domain target signature but simultaneously introduce statistical uncertainty due to their unknown realizations. Simulations validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed detector, which highlights the necessity of designing a dedicated detector to fully exploit the signaling resources assigned to random data payloads.

papers.title: The BAR-SOT Method: Long-term Average Cost Control as Stochastic Optimal Self-Transport
papers.summary: We reformulate average-cost (ergodic) control of a Markov jump process as a finite-horizon stochastic optimal transport (SOT) problem that jointly optimizes over the controlled evolution and the marginal law from which it starts and returns to (i.e., a self-transport). The constraint relating the marginal flow to the controlled generator is the basic adjoint relationship (BAR), so we call the resulting problem BAR-SOT. For any time horizon T>0, its optimal value is a constant scaling of the long-run average-cost rate. We give three equivalent formulations (through controlled processes, a Fokker--Planck constraint, and relaxed marginal measures) and show that the optimal dual is a stationary potential plus a term linear in time, with slope equal to the rate. A relative-entropy penalty on the control yields a cost-tilted Schrodinger bridge problem, computable by a Sinkhorn-type iteration when every transition rate is controlled, whose value converges to the unregularized optimum as the penalty vanishes. We develop the theory for finite Markov decision processes and then for general controlled Markov jump processes. A neural parametrization of the dual, trained as a physics-informed neural network (PINN), that encodes Harrison's equivalent-workload formulation (see Harrison 2000) matches the strong reinforcement-learning baseline of Dai and Gluzman (2022); numerically conditioning the fit of a sub-dominant transverse correction then improves on both that baseline and the best priority heuristic. On the input-queued switch, a graph-attention parametrization of the dual improves on the strongest matching heuristic we are aware of, with a parameter count that does not grow with the switch size.

papers.title: Safe Leader-Follower Density Control via Higher-Order Mean-Field Control Barrier Functions
papers.summary: Mean-field control barrier functions (MF-CBFs) enforce safety of large-scale multi-agent systems at the level of densities, but existing formulations require the control to act directly on the population to be kept safe. We consider populations that are not directly actuated and are influenced only through other, controlled populations, possibly in the presence of diffusion. We show that if the constrained population lies at directed graph distance d from the actuated one, then, under a nondegeneracy condition, the safety functional has relative degree d+1 and the control enters its (d+1)-th time derivative affinely. Higher-order safety constraints can therefore still be enforced through a convex quadratic program. We apply the framework to leader-follower density control among dangerous regions, where the follower safety functional has relative degree two and the leader safety functional has relative degree one. We characterize exactly when the two constraints are jointly infeasible and bound the tracking errors induced by the safety correction. Simulations in cluttered environments show that the proposed filter preserves follower safety, whereas enforcing leader safety alone does not.

papers.title: Commanding at the Speed of Sound: Audio-Centric Referring Expression Segmentation for Aerial Scenes
papers.summary: Referring expression segmentation (RES) aims to localize targets at the pixel level guided by human instructions. However, current models predominantly follow a text-centric paradigm that treats discrete text as the primary interaction medium for these human instructions. This assumption is especially limiting in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, where rapid response, hands-free operation, and natural communication are often critical. In this paper, we reconstruct UAV referring expression segmentation through an audio-centric perspective. Grounded in information theory, we demonstrate that raw audio provides a higher upper bound for extracting rich semantic features than transcribed text. To achieve this, we construct an audio-driven UAV referring expression segmentation benchmark named Aerial-AudioRES by augmenting VisDrone with synthesized speech, forming "audio-text-image-mask" quadruples. Specifically, we employ an ambiguity filtering mechanism to ensure referential uniqueness, and incorporate eight distinct timbres alongside 4 realistic noises to simulate authentic environments. To drive the paradigm shift from text-centric to audio-centric, we propose the end-to-end Audio-centric Referring Expression Segmentation Network (ARES-Net). Distinct from discrete text-visual matching, our approach learns to establish a direct soft alignment between continuous acoustic manifolds and multi-scale visual representations. Comprehensive experiments show that our method obtains a peak accuracy of 64.23% in oIoU and demonstrates robust generalization on a collected real-human test set. Furthermore, it significantly reduces total interaction latency to one-third of the text-based method. Our code is available at https://github.com/LemonGauss/ARES-Net.
